title: スパイ容疑の女性、AIチップ取引を売り込み

sources.headline: Thursday briefing: What we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang and the Nvidia affair
sources.text:
Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines.Five big stories
UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand.
Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.
US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.
Europe | Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
Technology | Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.
In depth: Everything we know (or don’t) about the Nvidia affairUS intelligence officials had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang. Photograph: CTI/AFPTV/AFP/Getty ImagesLast month, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, the former executive of a Singapore-based computing company, Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia; it buys the extremely valuable chips they produce, which are essential for powering AI, and rents computing space to Chinese companies. The US government had already been investigating whether Megaspeed could be flouting US restrictions and smuggling chips into China – allegations that both Nvidia and Megaspeed deny.US intelligence officials, who had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, eventually concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had been passing on information to Beijing. The intelligence behind this assessment is classified, so we don’t know exactly what they found – or which intelligence body was conducting the surveillance. Nvidia said Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected”, but on Sunday, Huang admitted in a letter to his employees that he had been having an affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children,” he said, adding that he was “deeply sorry”.Nvidia’s valuation is inextricably linked to Huang. By yesterday, $430bn (5.5%) had been wiped off its share price, and in the early hours of this morning, that figure ballooned to about $600bn following reports that Nvidia’s board was deciding whether to oust Huang (you can follow the latest on that here). The company has appointed outside counsel to review the pair’s relationship and says it has no reason to believe that secrets or national security were compromised.The most interesting aspects of this story are the questions we can’t (yet) answer. Did Nvidia’s board know that US intelligence suspected Alice Huang was a spy? What evidence led US intelligence to conclude she was spying for China? What information could she have passed to Beijing? And …Who is Alice Huang?Reporters and sleuths on Chinese social media have been trying to get to the bottom of who the Megaspeed chief really is. On Tuesday, the Financial Times published an interesting report (£) about Alice Huang’s backstory. She was born in the rural area of Hunan, worked as a journalist at China’s state broadcaster, then at HSBC and the investment bank Citic Securities. In 2015, she joined an investment management company Hexi.There, she met financier Kang Wei. The two became romantically involved, and together they reinvented themselves as AI entrepreneurs. In 2023, Huang and her business partners acquired Megaspeed, a Singaporean subsidiary of a Chinese gaming company, which she and Wei aimed to turn into a datacentre business. According to the FT’s report, the two pitched investors on their ability to secure access to Nvidia chips.Nobody knows exactly when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, when their relationship became romantic, or what information she might have passed to Beijing while it was going on. The earliest picture of them together is at an after-party following a tech trade show in Taipei, taken in 2024. As Aisha Down and Dan Milmo pointed out earlier this week, Jensen Huang is close to Donald Trump, so it’s possible that Alice Huang could have gained glimpses into US AI policy as it was being formed, into Trump’s thinking on AI, or into Nvidia’s company strategy. But without seeing the evidence, all this is speculation.What does this reveal about Chinese espionage?The US has been historically cautious about allowing AI chips to end up in Chinese hands. In 2022, Joe Biden’s administration introduced the Chips and Science Act, which restricted the sale of US chips in China, banning the export of most Nvidia chips. “The Chinese have a very strong pedigree for industrial espionage and copying other nations’ technologies,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute, tells me. “They’ve been doing this for decades. And now it’s no longer engines they’re interested in, but AI.”Both the US and China have an interest in gathering intelligence about each other’s AI firms. What’s more remarkable is the possibility that the Chinese spy agency, the MSS, could have recruited Alice Huang as a “honeytrap” to ensnare Jensen Huang – a method fraught with risk, which seems more reminiscent of 1970s spy fiction than contemporary counterintelligence (China, for its part, has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a spy).“The facts clearly aren’t established, but it seems more likely that if Alice Huang was working for Beijing, the MSS would have recruited her after they became aware of her relationship with Huang, not before,” Nigel Inkster, the former director of operations and intelligence for the British Secret Intelligence Service, tells me.China has built a large intelligence gathering operation: the MSS is now bigger than the CIA, and various national security laws mean that Chinese nationals can be required to provide assistance to the Chinese state. “You have a lot of people who can be co-opted into intelligence gathering, all of whom can be tasked with different requirements,” Inkster says. “Business delegations travelling abroad can be tasked with gathering information. So can visiting academics.”“The big question, to my mind, is whether the Chinese intelligence agencies have actually been willing to deliver unwelcome information to the party leadership,” Inkster adds.What approach has the US taken?Jensen Huang is the most influential figure in the US AI industry outside major labs such as Anthropic, and has cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump. He’s successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen regulations on AI and roll back restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China (last year, Trump controversially approved the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips directly to China in exchange for the federal government taking a 25% cut). Huang was present at the White House twice last month: once for a state dinner with Xi Jinping, and again for a meeting of tech and AI executives.Huang’s close relationship with Trump could help explain why the president has so far played down concerns about Chinese espionage, appearing remarkably ambivalent about the recent allegations. The president was reportedly briefed last year about US intelligence conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, and in spring this year, his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, supervised the drafting of a classified memo warning that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with a Chinese spy. In May, Trump issued a last-minute invitation to Jensen Huang to board Air Force One in Alaska and join a delegation of executives bound to China. A US government official told reporters at the New York Times that when Rubio learned that Huang would be joining the trip in Alaska, he briefed Trump on the memo.But on Monday, Trump, who is due to meet Xi Jinping later this month, said he had not known at the time of the trip about Huang’s relationship. He said the FBI had been investigating a matter relating to Huang, and defended the Nvidia CEO, describing

sources.headline: Who is Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy linked to Nvidia's Jensen Huang?
sources.text:
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese businesswoman who has been at the centre of allegations involving a suspected Chinese intelligence operation targeting Nvidia and its former CEO, Jensen Huang.
US intelligence agencies believed she had been recruited by Beijing to gather information on one of the world's most valuable technology companies. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang share a surname but are not related.
She previously held a senior position at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data centre company that rents computing power to businesses developing and running AI systems. Megaspeed described itself as a key business partner of Nvidia's cloud computing operations in the Asia-Pacific region.
Photographs from a technology industry event in 2024 showed the two sitting together. In May 2025, they also attended a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang in Taipei during the Computex technology expo.
Video footage from the restaurant showed Jensen Huang putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kissed him on the cheek. They were later seen leaving in the same car.
Jensen Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues. Nvidia's board subsequently launched an independent investigation into the matter.
On Thursday, November 12, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO and board member after 33 years leading the company. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO.
Separately, Singapore's authorities confirmed that Alice Huang had been investigated over possible offences involving the purchase and export of servers through Singapore. She left the country in February and was subsequently barred from re-entering. Authorities said the investigation was not related to espionage and that there was insufficient evidence to establish that she had committed an offence. She was issued a stern warning over information provided to investigators.

sources.headline: Megaspeed ex-CEO Alice Huang barred from Singapore amid Nvidia saga
sources.text: Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, accused by the US of being a Chinese spy and linked to an extramarital affair with tech giant Nvidia’s co-founder Jensen Huang, has been barred from re-entering Singapore over inaccurate information provided to police. Alice Huang, a Hong Kong resident, was found to have downplayed her role in Megaspeed in investigations by Singapore police, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) said in a statement on Thursday. sources.headline: Who is the suspected Chinese spy at centre of the Nvidia investigation?
sources.text: US chip giant Nvidia has said it is investigating reports that its CEO Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who had been the managing director of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.The New York Times reported that US officials suspect Alice Huang has been working for China's spy agency to collect intelligence. China has denied allegations of Huang being a Chinese spy, calling the allegations "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." Nvidia says it has no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, but will "examine all available information". Asia reporter Tessa Wong explains what we know about Alice Huang, and her links to Jensen Huang.

sources.headline: Alice Huang boasted about Nvidia AI chip access to investors, told them Alibaba would be a client for the project
sources.text: Alice Huang boasted to her investors that she would have no problem accessing Nvidia's AI chip for her upcoming project.Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy linked to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, pitched a multimillion-dollar artificial intelligence infrastructure project to investors, claiming she could secure the US company's advanced chips and citing Chinese technology giant Alibaba as a prospective client, according to a Financial Times report.Alice Huang and her business partner Kang Wei sought investment in early 2025 for a Southeast Asian data-centre project estimated to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars, the FT reported, citing two investors who were approached about the proposal.During the pitch, the pair said they had no problem securing Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs), a key component used to develop and operate artificial intelligence systems. They also cited Alibaba as a client for the proposed project, according to an investor familiar with the discussions.The development adds another dimension to the scrutiny surrounding Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, following allegations that she was recruited by Chinese intelligence to establish a relationship with Jensen Huang and potentially influence his position on US restrictions on advanced chip exports to China.The allegations have not been independently established. Beijing has rejected the espionage claims, while Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing related to chip smuggling.Questions over Nvidia chips and China linksThe proposed data-centre project also raises questions about how advanced Nvidia chips could be made available to Chinese businesses through infrastructure located outside mainland China.US export controls restrict Chinese companies from owning certain advanced AI chips, although Chinese businesses can lease computing capacity from data centres operating overseas, subject to applicable restrictions.The FT report said Alice Huang and Kang Wei presented access to Nvidia GPUs as a central part of their investment proposal. Their reference to Alibaba also drew attention to the Chinese technology company's reported business relationship with Megaspeed.Documents reviewed by the FT investigation showed that Alibaba had lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries in 2024. People familiar with the company described Alibaba as Megaspeed's anchor customer and largest client.Jensen Huang faces growing scrutinyThe latest revelations come as Nvidia faces questions over its chief executive's reported relationship with Alice Huang and whether the company was exposed to a potential foreign intelligence operation.US intelligence officials reportedly believe Alice Huang was connected to a Chinese espionage effort targeting Jensen Huang. The alleged objective was to gather information about the Nvidia chief and influence his efforts to persuade Washington to ease restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an extramarital affair and apologized to his wife and family. Nvidia's independent directors have launched an investigation into whether he was targeted in a foreign intelligence operation.The company has said it has no reason to believe that its national security interests or confidential information were compromised. The allegations have nevertheless brought renewed attention to Nvidia's business dealings in China and the security implications of its global AI chip supply chain.

sources.headline: Honey traps: Sex, lies and a spy’s oldest trick
sources.text: PARIS – AI, superchips and cyber warfare may be reshaping modern espionage, but some secrets are still won the old-fashioned way: through sex and scandal.The latest controversy to ripple through the tech world centres on Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and his affair with a woman accused by Washington of working for Chinese intelligence, a claim Beijing denies.The episode has thrust the “honey trap” back into the spotlight, reviving interest in an age-old spying tactic that turns attraction and intimacy into tools for stealing state secrets and influencing those in power.Seduction and blackmailHistory is packed with powerful politicians and insiders who found themselves ensnared by men and women tasked with winning their trust before extracting intelligence or gaining leverage.One of the most famous femme fatales in spy lore is Mata Hari, the Dutch exotic dancer executed in 1917 after being accused of spying for Germany during World War I.The Cold War also produced a long list of similarly colourful cases.In France, ambassador Maurice Dejean was recalled from Moscow in 1964 after an extramarital affair, said Clement Renault, a researcher at France’s Institute for Strategic Research (IRSEM).The scandal created one of former president Charles de Gaulle’s most memorable put-downs: “Alors Dejean, on couche?” (“So, Dejean, sleeping around?”).Another famous case, Renault said, involved the Soviet KGB blackmailing British embassy employee John Vassall with “intimate photos revealing his homosexuality, taken in Moscow”.In the 1980s, Israeli whistleblower Mordechai Vanunu, who revealed details of Israel’s secret nuclear programme, was lured into the hands of his kidnappers by a woman known as “Cindy”.She “persuaded him to join her in Rome, where he was abducted by the Mossad and taken back to Israel,” Renault explained.Other honey traps ran for years.In the 1960s, Chinese opera singer Shi Pei Pu, secretly working for Chinese intelligence, began a two-decade affair with French diplomat Bernard Boursicot, who handed over sensitive information.Not so glamorousThe honey trap can take many forms.Some seducers are trained professionals, like East Germany’s famed “Romeo Spies” whose mission was to romance lonely West German women and gain access to important information.“With the shortage of eligible men – another consequence of the war (WWII) – single West German women, eager for male companionship, became frequent targets for East German male spies,” the CIA later said in a study.Not every honey trap looks like something out of a Hollywood film.Intelligence services have also used sex workers, business executives and well-connected individuals who already move in the target’s world.That is what makes the Nvidia allegations so intriguing.Alice Huang, the woman involved in the affair, “held a senior role at Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm specialising in AI computing infrastructure” that did business with Nvidia, Renault said.“She was allegedly recruited by (China’s) state security ministry as an agent, perfectly placed to make contact (with Jensen Huang),” Renault said.“What is interesting here is that a key figure in the ‘AI war’ could be caught in a relatively classic operation.”Some cases are not so subtle.A former member of a French security service recalled being contacted by a woman from South America who claimed she was a journalist seeking an interview with a senior security official.“I met her twice,” he told AFP.“Each time she was evasive about her work as a journalist and what the interview was actually about. But she kept telling me her marriage was unhappy and showing me photos of herself in lingerie.”Too good to be trueWho deploys honey traps? According to Renault, the short answer is almost everyone.“Potentially all intelligence services can resort to ‘compromise’ operations and similar methods,” Renault said.But not all states are equally equipped to run them.“These missions require an extremely high level of personal and physical commitment from agents”, Renault noted.So authoritarian governments, he argued, “which can exert greater pressure on their citizens or are driven by strong ideologies”, may be better positioned to ask agents to make such sacrifices.Counter-intelligence agencies regularly warn officials that espionage rarely begins with a dramatic exchange in a dark alley.France’s domestic service has released a YouTube video titled: “Trapped by a foreign intelligence agency. It’s never too late to get help.”The British authorities offer simpler advice.If someone’s interest in you seems unusually intense or “too good to be true”, then “you should be cautious”. AFP
